newsitem.title: Australia: CANBERRA WATCH-Evidence of a government playing safe.
newsitem.headline: CANBERRA WATCH-Evidence of a government playing safe.

text.p: Sydney's Daily Telegraph newspaper reports today that Prime Minister John Howard and Treasurer Peter Costello had a heated exchange over budget cuts last week.
The report, which Canberra Watch has been unable to confirm but which Costello has refused to deny, could be enormously important.

The Telegraph reported that Howard on Thursay vetoed a package of proposed budget measures that Costello and Finance Minister John Fahey had taken to cabinet's Expenditure Review Committee and the argument ensued.
Melbourne's Herald-Sun ran a similar report on Tuesday, but did not mention anyone losing his temper.
After finding A$7 billion in full-year cuts in last year's budget, it must be very tough to identify the further A$2 billion or more needed for this year.
No doubt Costello and Fahey had to sweat blood to find the unspecified package of cuts that Howard reportedly rejected.
Reporters quizzed Costello about the reported incident at some length at Wednesday's CPI news conference but never took the opportunity to flatly deny it.
The treasurer hid behind the excuse that such meetings are private affairs, but it would have been no great breach of protocol for him to simply say: "No such argument occured."
Instead, the nearest he came to denial was saying: "Some passionate reports from some journalists should not be taken as factual and I recommend for them a cold shower."
If the reports are true, Canberra watchers need to note two implications.
SMALLER RATHER THAN LARGER BUDGET CUTS
First, a Howard veto over budget measures implies that this year's cuts will tend to be smaller rather than larger.
Costello wouuld now seem less likely to pull a rabbit out of the hat and announce much bigger cuts than suggested before budget night.

The government's target is a balanced budget in 1998/99, ignoring asset sales and the like. On budget figuring issued in January, that will require measures that save A$2 billion in that fiscal year -- maybe something closer A$3 billion to be on the safe side.
(Incidentally, the latest government financial statistics raise no firm suggestion that Treasury's January fiscal forecasts are wrong in either direction.)
A POLL-DRIVEN GOVERNMENT
The second and larger implication is that the government may tend to play things politically safe rather than courageously, especially as the government's opinion-poll lead fades.
Many commentators have already labelled Howard as a poll-driven prime minister, and there has been some evidence of the government becoming a little less brave in recent months.
A big factor here is the government's enormous backbench of probable oncers -- members of parliament who are likely to get one term only.
The potential oncers are terrified of politically brave measures and have no doubt pressured the prime minister at every opportunity to play things safe.
The newspaper reports suggest that they may be getting their way.
